title: Teacher development is messier than our models of it
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes draws on a review of 64 empirical studies of language teacher development (2008-2023) to argue that schools rely on frameworks that are too tidy, isolating identity, beliefs, emotion or agency when in practice these are entangled and shaped by context. She highlights the review's three recurring patterns: emotion drives agency, emotion and cognition shape each other, and their interaction influences agency for pedagogical change. From this she argues that professional development cannot be modelled as content plus delivery, since teachers may understand a reform yet resist it because of what it does to their identity, their emotions or their room to act. She positions reflective practice as the mediating mechanism that integrates these strands, not as a soft extra or a form-filling ritual. She also stresses that institutional and sociopolitical pressures featured more prominently than classroom concerns in the studies, which should prompt leaders to look at the culture around CPD. Her conclusion is that teacher development is identity work, and that treating it as knowledge transfer is both less effective and less honest.
points: Hughes's key argument is that teacher identity, cognition, emotion and agency develop together under pressure, so frameworks that isolate one factor misread why practice does not change.
She argues that emotion belongs inside CPD rather than in parallel wellbeing work, since anxiety, status threat or exhaustion can narrow thinking and weaken professional judgement.
Resistance to a reform is reframed as a response to identity threat or constrained context rather than irrationality or lack of buy-in.
The review found meso- and macro-level institutional and sociopolitical pressures more prominent than classroom-level concerns, which puts school culture and leadership in the frame.
Reflection is presented as the mechanism by which teachers integrate feeling, understanding and action into coherent practice.
quotes: One of the persistent problems in teacher development is that we keep trying to explain it with frameworks that are too tidy. We isolate one thing at a time, like teacher identity, teacher beliefs, teacher emotion and teacher agency.
They are entangled. Teachers do not think first, then feel, then act, then revise their identity. These processes happen together, often under pressure.

This is perhaps why even good professional development can fall flat. A teacher may understand the rationale behind a reform and still resist it, not because they are irrational, but because the reform threatens a valued professional identity, generates emotional strain, or sits in a context that makes meaningful action difficult.

A reform that creates chronic anxiety, status threat, moral discomfort, or exhaustion is not just emotionally costly. It may also narrow thinking, distort professional judgement, and reduce the teacher’s capacity to act agentively.

Reflection is sometimes treated in schools as either a soft extra or a ritual. Teachers are asked to reflect at the end of a session, fill in a form, or take part in a coaching conversation, but the reflective work is not always taken seriously as a mechanism of development.

That should make school leaders pause. Many development models still focus narrowly on practice inside the classroom while paying too little attention to the surrounding context that shapes whether development is possible in the first place.

Teachers are not changed simply by being told better things. They are shaped by the interaction of what they think, what they feel, how they see themselves, what room they have to act, and the institutional world around them. That makes professional development harder to design, certainly.
